messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 71
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Oceania
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Painter
- Trauma Type: Terrorism
- Pcl5: 48

He lives alone in a small house at the edge of town, the kind with a corrugated iron roof and a wooden porch that looks out toward the ocean. He has lived here for almost forty years, ever since he moved to this island as a young man. The house is cluttered with half-finished canvases, tubes of oil paint, and brushes that he cleans every evening with a patient, almost ritualistic care. He paints every day, usually from early morning until the light fades, but he no longer paints what he used to.

Before, he painted the market. He loved the market. He would set up his easel near the fish stalls or the fruit vendors, mixing bright yellows and reds and greens, trying to catch the way sunlight hit a pile of mangoes or the glint of a knife as a fishmonger scaled a catch. People knew him there. They would stop and look at his work, sometimes buy a small canvas to hang in their homes. He was known as the painter who captured the life of the village.

That morning, he was at the market. It was a Tuesday, he remembers, because Tuesdays were less crowded. He was working on a painting of a woman selling woven baskets. The explosion came from somewhere near the bus stop. He does not remember the sound, only the pressure, the way the air seemed to turn solid and then push him sideways into a pile of burlap sacks. When he opened his eyes, there was dust everywhere and a ringing in his ears, and someone was screaming. He tried to stand but his legs would not hold him. He saw a man he knew—a baker, a quiet man who always gave him free bread—lying on the ground, not moving.

He was helped to a clinic. His eardrum was ruptured in one ear, and he had cuts from flying debris, but nothing broken. The physical wounds healed. The hearing in that ear never fully returned.

Now, he stays home. He cannot go to the market. Even the thought of it makes his chest tighten and his hands begin to tremble. He tried once, about a year after the bombing, but he made it only as far as the edge of the square before his vision started to blur and he had to turn back. He has not tried again. He buys his food from a small store a few blocks from his house, one that never has more than two or three customers at a time. He goes early, before the crowds.

He still paints, but the colors have changed. He uses more grey now, more brown. He paints the sea at dusk, the shape of rocks, the empty spaces between things. He paints the view from his porch, over and over, because it is safe. He does not paint people anymore. Once, he tried to paint a figure, just a silhouette in the distance, but his hand shook so badly he could not control the brush. He set the canvas aside and has not touched it since.

At night, he has trouble sleeping. He lies awake and listens to the wind or the creak of the house, and sometimes he hears the sound that is not a sound, the impossible pressure of an explosion that happened eight years ago. He gets up and walks through the dark rooms, checking the locks, even though he knows they are secure. There is no danger here, he tells himself. But his body does not believe it.

He has a daughter who lives on the mainland. She calls every Sunday. He tells her he is fine, that he is painting, that the weather is good. He does not tell her about the dreams, or the way he startles when a truck backfires, or how he sometimes stops mid-stroke and stares at the canvas without remembering what he was doing. He does not tell her that he feels as though part of him is still lying on that ground, in the dust, waiting for someone to help him stand.

The PCL-5 score of 48 means little to him. He only knows that his life has narrowed to this small house, to these quiet mornings, to the steady work of filling a white surface with color. He is still a painter. He is just painting a different world now.
